title: Our journey into AI gamedev - here are the results so far
author: GigaBrainTactics

comments.author: Fair_External8606
comments.body:
If two people with no game development experience really pulled this off, I take my hat off to you, Sir!   
You definitely have the taste to bring AI art together into such a pleasing composition. I hope the gameplay feels just as good in the refined version of the game. Added it to my wishlist, good luck with the development guys!

replies.author: GigaBrainTactics
replies.body:
Thank you so much for wishlisting the game! ❤️

Yeah, I think a lot of people still underestimate what AI is capable of - while others overestimate it and end up disappointed when they realize they can’t create an entire game “with a single prompt.”

Just like with any other tool, you still need to learn, experiment, and figure out how to adapt modern AI tools to solve the specific problems you’re facing. If you do that, they can be incredibly powerful.

Throughout development, we’ve actually started over almost from scratch several times. We kept learning new things, discovering better approaches, and then adapting what we learned to the project.

We’ll definitely do our best to make GIGA BRAIN TACTICS a fun and interesting game!

We’re currently planning to release the demo in time for Steam Next Fest in October. 🚀

comments.author: rookan
comments.body: How did you generate monsters? Their artstyle is beautiful! Especially succubus girl.

replies.author: GigaBrainTactics
replies.body:
Thank you! The Succubus is one of our favorites too :)

We actually used pretty much every AI tool we could get our hands on during development. Our main tools have been **ChatGPT/Codex and Claude**, usually using the latest models available at the time. With Claude we mostly used Opus rather than Fable, and Codex became noticeably better for our workflow after Astra arrived.

For the visual side, though, it wasn't really a case of typing one prompt and getting a finished character.

My teammate often starts with a graphics tablet and makes a very rough sketch first -  sometimes literally just simple lines showing the pose, proportions, silhouette and where different elements should be. We then use that as a visual reference so the AI has a much clearer idea of what we're trying to achieve instead of describing everything with text alone.

This approach has been especially useful for UI, but we also use the same general idea when working on characters and other visual elements.

Then it's a lot of iteration: generate a prototype → see what's wrong → adjust the reference/prompt → generate again. Once we have something close to what we want, some assets are additionally edited manually in Photoshop.

So even though AI is heavily involved in our art pipeline, we've basically never had a situation where **one prompt = finished asset**. Even when the initial result looks great, there are almost always details that need another iteration or manual cleanup.

That's pretty much been our experience with AI throughout the whole project: it's extremely useful for getting from an idea to something tangible very quickly, but getting from **“this looks promising” to “this is exactly what we want in the game”** still takes quite a bit of work.

replies.author: rookan
replies.body: Thanks for reply. How did you do characters animations? AI also? Which model?

replies.author: GigaBrainTactics
replies.body:
Yes, AI as well :) We used **Grok** for the character animations.

Just like with the artwork, it usually took several iterations to get the movement we wanted - the first result was rarely the final one.
